# A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. Much of past research in this area has examined the barriers to error reporting. This research has helped identify common structural barriers to error reporting, such as the complicated and time-consuming nature of error reporting systems, as well as knowledge deficits of what constitutes an error or a near miss (Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . Other studies have identified cultural and managerial barriers, and common fears about reporting errors that are often shared across different types of employees (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) .

While past studies have produced important findings, these findings have not fully explained how more complex factors within the organisation may affect error reporting by clinicians. Theory and research from organisational and team literature may help to better explain the more complex reasons as to why clinicians do or do not report errors, in a way that past research on error reporting has failed to do. The team literature is especially relevant when studying error reporting by nurses because nurses typically work within nursing units or departments (i.e. surgical intensive care unit, emergency department, labour and delivery, etc.) thus creating a team atmosphere with distinct cultures and norms.

## Team dynamics in relation to error reporting

Safety climate represents the shared perceptions and experiences of employees about the practices, policies and procedures that contribute to patient safety (Katz-Navon et al., 2005; Vogus and Sutcliffe, 2007) . Safety climate and safety culture are commonly interchanged in the literature, which makes previous research on both safety climate and safety culture relevant to this study (Mearns and Flin, 1999; Zaheer et al., 2015) . Past research demonstrates that positive perceptions of employees about the safety climate and safety culture on their work units and in their organisations are associated with improved safety practices and fewer errors (Berry et al., 2020; Hofmann and Mark, 2006; Naveh et al., 2005) , increased levels of error reporting (Fox et al., 2017; Kagan and Barnoy, 2013; Naveh et al., 2006) , a greater willingness to report errors (Lee et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2013; Yoo and Kim, 2017) and more positive perceptions about error reporting (Richter et al., 2015) .

Past studies of error reporting have also highlighted the important relationship between leadership behaviours and error reporting by employees. In particular, leader inclusiveness, defined as the availability, openness and accessibility of leaders, is demonstrated when leaders invite input from employees and offer appreciation for their contributions (Hirak et al., 2012; Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The concept of leader inclusiveness was first introduced by Nembhard and Edmondson in a study examining the effect of professional status on staff perceptions of psychological safety when involved in quality improvement efforts in neonatal intensive care units (Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The researchers found that more inclusive leadership positively predicted team engagement in quality improvement work. A more recent study focusing on error reporting found that higher levels of leader inclusiveness among attending physicians positively influenced the reporting behaviours of resident physicians (Appelbaum et al., 2016) .

Psychological safety has been defined as 'individuals' perceptions about the consequences of interpersonal risks in their work environment. It consists of taken-for-granted beliefs about how others will respond when one puts oneself on the line, such as by asking a question, seeking feedback, reporting a mistake or proposing a new idea' (Edmondson, 2004) . Psychological safety conveys the extent to which team members feel safe or are fearful in identifying and speaking up about problems they encounter in their work, including error reporting (Edmondson, 1999 (Edmondson, , 2004)) . Research on error reporting indicates that fear is consistently identified as a significant barrier to reporting (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . As a result, it seems that fear related to error reporting may be manifest as poor psychological safety on the part of clinicians, thus inhibiting them from reporting errors. Studies examining psychological safety and error reporting have found a significant relationship between psychological safety and error reporting or speaking up behaviours (Appelbaum et al., 2016; Derickson et al., 2015; Leroy et al., 2012; Sherf et al., 2021) .

turning to the rose-tree, she went on, “What _have_ you been doing
here?”

“May it please your Majesty,” said Two, in a very humble tone, going
down on one knee as he spoke, “we were trying—”

“_I_ see!” said the Queen, who had meanwhile been examining the roses.
“Off with their heads!” and the procession moved on, three of the
soldiers remaining behind to execute the unfortunate gardeners, who ran
to Alice for protection.

“You shan’t be beheaded!” said Alice, and she put them into a large
flower-pot that stood near. The three soldiers wandered about for a
minute or two, looking for them, and then quietly marched off after the
others.

“Are their heads off?” shouted the Queen.

“Their heads are gone, if it please your Majesty!” the soldiers shouted
in reply.

“That’s right!” shouted the Queen. “Can you play croquet?”

The soldiers were silent, and looked at Alice, as the question was
evidently meant for her.

“Yes!” shouted Alice.

“Come on, then!” roared the Queen, and Alice joined the procession,
wondering very much what would happen next.

walking by the White Rabbit, who was peeping anxiously into her face.

“Very,” said Alice: “—where’s the Duchess?”

“Hush! Hush!” said the Rabbit in a low, hurried tone. He looked
anxiously over his shoulder as he spoke, and then raised himself upon
tiptoe, put his mouth close to her ear, and whispered “She’s under
sentence of execution.”

“What for?” said Alice.

“Did you say ‘What a pity!’?” the Rabbit asked.

# A study of error reporting by nurses: the significant impact of nursing team dynamics

## Abstract

Background: Error reporting is crucial for organisational learning and improving patient safety in hospitals, yet errors are significantly underreported. Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Methods: The study was a cross-sectional design. Self-administered surveys were used to collect data from nurses and nurse managers. Data were analysed using linear mixed models. Bootstrap confidence intervals with bias correction were used for mediation analysis. Results: Leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety significantly affected willingness to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. Much of past research in this area has examined the barriers to error reporting. This research has helped identify common structural barriers to error reporting, such as the complicated and time-consuming nature of error reporting systems, as well as knowledge deficits of what constitutes an error or a near miss (Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . Other studies have identified cultural and managerial barriers, and common fears about reporting errors that are often shared across different types of employees (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) .

While past studies have produced important findings, these findings have not fully explained how more complex factors within the organisation may affect error reporting by clinicians. Theory and research from organisational and team literature may help to better explain the more complex reasons as to why clinicians do or do not report errors, in a way that past research on error reporting has failed to do. The team literature is especially relevant when studying error reporting by nurses because nurses typically work within nursing units or departments (i.e. surgical intensive care unit, emergency department, labour and delivery, etc.) thus creating a team atmosphere with distinct cultures and norms.

## Team dynamics in relation to error reporting

Safety climate represents the shared perceptions and experiences of employees about the practices, policies and procedures that contribute to patient safety (Katz-Navon et al., 2005; Vogus and Sutcliffe, 2007) . Safety climate and safety culture are commonly interchanged in the literature, which makes previous research on both safety climate and safety culture relevant to this study (Mearns and Flin, 1999; Zaheer et al., 2015) . Past research demonstrates that positive perceptions of employees about the safety climate and safety culture on their work units and in their organisations are associated with improved safety practices and fewer errors (Berry et al., 2020; Hofmann and Mark, 2006; Naveh et al., 2005) , increased levels of error reporting (Fox et al., 2017; Kagan and Barnoy, 2013; Naveh et al., 2006) , a greater willingness to report errors (Lee et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2013; Yoo and Kim, 2017) and more positive perceptions about error reporting (Richter et al., 2015) .

Past studies of error reporting have also highlighted the important relationship between leadership behaviours and error reporting by employees. In particular, leader inclusiveness, defined as the availability, openness and accessibility of leaders, is demonstrated when leaders invite input from employees and offer appreciation for their contributions (Hirak et al., 2012; Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The concept of leader inclusiveness was first introduced by Nembhard and Edmondson in a study examining the effect of professional status on staff perceptions of psychological safety when involved in quality improvement efforts in neonatal intensive care units (Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) . The researchers found that more inclusive leadership positively predicted team engagement in quality improvement work. A more recent study focusing on error reporting found that higher levels of leader inclusiveness among attending physicians positively influenced the reporting behaviours of resident physicians (Appelbaum et al., 2016) .

Psychological safety has been defined as 'individuals' perceptions about the consequences of interpersonal risks in their work environment. It consists of taken-for-granted beliefs about how others will respond when one puts oneself on the line, such as by asking a question, seeking feedback, reporting a mistake or proposing a new idea' (Edmondson, 2004) . Psychological safety conveys the extent to which team members feel safe or are fearful in identifying and speaking up about problems they encounter in their work, including error reporting (Edmondson, 1999 (Edmondson, , 2004)) . Research on error reporting indicates that fear is consistently identified as a significant barrier to reporting (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . As a result, it seems that fear related to error reporting may be manifest as poor psychological safety on the part of clinicians, thus inhibiting them from reporting errors. Studies examining psychological safety and error reporting have found a significant relationship between psychological safety and error reporting or speaking up behaviours (Appelbaum et al., 2016; Derickson et al., 2015; Leroy et al., 2012; Sherf et al., 2021) .

Aims: The aim of this study was to understand how the nursing team dynamics of leader inclusiveness, safety climate and psychological safety affected the willingness of hospital nurses to report errors. Psychological safety mediated the relationship between safety climate and error reporting as well as the relationship between leader inclusiveness and error reporting.

## Introduction

Hospitals depend on employees to meaningfully contribute to quality improvement efforts by engaging in actions that foster organisational learning. Error reporting is a primary tool by which hospitals learn from mistakes and near misses that occur during the delivery of patient care. However, error reporting requires some degree of risk, whether real or perceived, on the part of the individuals who report error (Newman et al., 2017) . The existing literature demonstrates that errors and near misses in hospitals are significantly underreported (Levinson, 2012; Palmero et al., 2019; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Yung et al., 2016) . As a result, countless opportunities to improve patient care quality and safety are lost because some employees do not report errors and near misses when they occur. In this study, we examined how team dynamics on nursing units affected error reporting by nurses.

## Literature review

Error reporting is multifaceted, with myriad reasons that explain why the process of error reporting often breaks down. Much of past research in this area has examined the barriers to error reporting. This research has helped identify common structural barriers to error reporting, such as the complicated and time-consuming nature of error reporting systems, as well as knowledge deficits of what constitutes an error or a near miss (Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) . Other studies have identified cultural and managerial barriers, and common fears about reporting errors that are often shared across different types of employees (Hewitt et al., 2017; Rashed and Hamdan, 2019; Rutledge et al., 2018; Vrbnjak et al., 2016) .

While past studies have produced important findings, these findings have not fully explained how more complex factors within the organisation may affect error reporting by clinicians. Theory and research from organisational and team literature may help to better explain the more complex reasons as to why clinicians do or do not report errors, in a way that past research on error reporting has failed to do. The team literature is especially relevant when studying error reporting by nurses because nurses typically work within nursing units or departments (i.e. surgical intensive care unit, emergency department, labour and delivery, etc.) thus creating a team atmosphere with distinct cultures and norms.

## Team dynamics in relation to error reporting

Safety climate represents the shared perceptions and experiences of employees about the practices, policies and procedures that contribute to patient safety (Katz-Navon et al., 2005; Vogus and Sutcliffe, 2007) . Safety climate and safety culture are commonly interchanged in the literature, which makes previous research on both safety climate and safety culture relevant to this study (Mearns and Flin, 1999; Zaheer et al., 2015) . The researchers found that more inclusive leadership positively predicted team engagement in quality improvement work. A more recent study focusing on error reporting found that higher levels of leader inclusiveness among attending physicians positively influenced the reporting behaviours of resident physicians (Appelbaum et al., 2016) .
